segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: My English name is Charlie Shell, in Cherokee it’s Hummingbird.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What is your name in English?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: My English name is Patsy Reese, in Cherokee it’s U-da-yi.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: My English name is James Adam Reese, Cherokee name is Tsa-gi.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where were you born?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: I was born in Tahlequah, but we lived in Rocky Ford.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Rocky Ford.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where’s that at?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Rocky Ford.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you know what Tsi-s-da-no-ya means?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Crawdads? [laughing]
[all laughing]

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: [laughing] Where crawdads live.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Crawdads come from.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You don’t know where the name Tsi-s-da-no-ya came from? OK.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you, where were you born?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Briggs.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Briggs?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What is Briggs in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: I really don’t know. I’ve only heard a-tsi-ni di-tli-gv. I know that’s what they call it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s what I’ve heard.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is that where you were raised, near Rocky Ford?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Yes, near there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Your parents live there – have they always live there?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Yes, we all lived there. Grandpa and Grandma, we all lived close by.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What were their names?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Their English name were Steve and Annie Wilson.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you know their Cherokee names?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: e-li-si and du-du [all laughing]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: My grandfather was John Dreadfulwater. My grandmother, Mary. I don’t know their Cherokee names; I never heard them before.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What do you do to help yourself, in your job?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: What I do in my job, I help them when they want something. I even help Cherokee speakers.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where do you work?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Clinic.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, what about you?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: I don’t work. I’m retired.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You’re retired?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did you do when you were working?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: I worked at the casino when I was working.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long did you work there?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: At the casino?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Oh, about 10 years, maybe.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And you are still working.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Uh-uh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long have you worked there?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: About three years there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you use to work at Housing Authority?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Yes, I worked there a long time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, I remember you working there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many was in your family?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Six.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you all talk Cherokee?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Yes, we all spoke Cherokee, but the younger boy understood Cherokee but didn’t speak it. He was the only one who didn’t speak it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You don’t know why?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: I guess when the older ones went to school and come back home, we spoke English and I guess that’s where he learned and started speaking English. He didn’t speak Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you were growing up, that’s all you spoke – Cherokee?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: We talked both.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Both?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you, how many were there?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Six.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Six?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you all speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: No, the younger three can understand it, but can’t speak it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They never tried?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: No, I don’t think so.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s where you were born, in Briggs?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you all live there, or did some move away?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: They just all grew up there – Mother or Grandma, they gave me the land. They gave me land a long time ago. That’s where they lived.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was that an allotment?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: 160 acres?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you live in a place like that? Not really?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Where I grew up, my dad worked in Tulsa. That’s when something happened to him. That’s when the insurance paid him, and he bought a house and on our land, that’s where we grew up.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What kind of work did he do?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: I really don’t know. I wasn’t born yet.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He was working in Tulsa.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Yeah, he worked in Tulsa.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: As children you never went over there [Tulsa]?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Uh-uh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When I first went over there, boy it was a long ways, now you get there pretty quick. [laughing]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Probably the same for you. Was he working to help the family? What was your father’s job?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Railroad – Kansas City Railroad.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long did he work there?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: I really don’t know…[inaudible]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did you think about growing up? Myself we weren’t doing well, but we came through it OK. What did you think about that time while you were growing up?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Myself, I didn’t think about it. Where we lived, we lived way out in the woods. I stayed around the water near the house. That’s the way it was back then.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Me either. We used to just hang around the water. We used to swim all the time.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: They would catch crawdads all the time, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you know each other back then?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you find her at?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: The first time I saw her. Remember? When the All-Indian tournament, baseball they were playing at Northeastern?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: That’s when.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Awww. Were you playing?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: I was just watching. [all laughing]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you were watching her instead of the ball game. [all laughing]

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Your grandmother and grandfather, did you know them? What was their names?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: My who?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Your grandmother and grandfather.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Yes, they were living. We used to visit with them. When we were children, we would visit with them. Right by the water, we would swim next to the church. We used to go there all the time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you go to church?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: New Mission.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: New Mission.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you, your grandmother and grandfather? Did you know them?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Yeah, a little bit. I was 11 years old when he died and my grandmother, too.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: She said, “You awake, you awake!” My grandmother would say, “Let’s speak Cherokee, let’s not speak English.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Not really.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: They spoke Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I understand what you are saying. Just about everyone I talk to they say they all go to the water. I guess they are about to get to water, they all gathered there you would say. That’s what a lot of them said.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they live where you were living?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: I really don’t know where they came from, when they got there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You don’t know either?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: I don’t know either. And I never even asked them. That’s the way it was when I was growing up.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you like your grandma’s cooking?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: I really did. She was always cooking. [all laughing]

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: My grandmother was mean. [laughing]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What food did she cook that you liked the most?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Chicken, I guess. She was a good cook.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: All of it. [all laughing]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you were kids, did you play? What did you use to play with?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Dolls and softball and sassafras stick.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you thought you were good?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Me, my aunt made it for us. She used socks that she would sew. Even strawberry in Stilwell they would pick. We would pick strawberries and then buy rubber balls they called them. We would go buy rubber balls we thought we were good now when we played ball.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you both remember what you did when you were growing up? Or were you just sitting around somewhere?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Sometimes. Wait, let’s see what we were doing when we were playing.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Jacks.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Yep, jacks.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You say jacks?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Yeah. Kick the can.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Yeah. Kick the can.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s what someone was telling me the other day, “What is kick the can?”

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: You set a trap and they hide and when the trapper is away then someone comes running out and kicks the can.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you pair up or did you play single?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Single.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You all fought for it or what?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: I forget how it goes, but if they caught that’s when you…

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Ooh, kick the can?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: You never heard of it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Someone mention that, but they didn’t explain what it was.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they tell you things, your parents or your grandparents or grandfather?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: When someone came to the house, we were sent outside so the grownups could talk. They would say, “You kids go outside.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How about you – was it the same?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: M-hm.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The same? That’s the way it was for us, “You go outside!” And if you got close that would chase you off.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Stick. [laughing]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was that?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Stick.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s right, they would get a stick or belt. [laughing]

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: They didn’t know. They called Granny ‘mom’. I didn’t find out until I was grown that they called Granny ‘mom’ until someone asked my grandmother why we called her ‘mom’. That’s what they used to say, I didn’t know, I called her mom all the time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: One of my sisters isn’t living now. They lived in Chicago for I don’t know how long. I didn’t know my sister. The reason is my other brother’s and sister’s friends would come over and when they came over they called my mom, ‘mom,’ too. When she came here from Chicago, she would call Mom ‘mom’. I didn’t believe she was my sister. I just figured it was people she knew. Later on, I found out she was my real sister.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How about now, your grandchildren, if you were to ask your grandma or grandpa something, would you want to ask them something? How about you?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: H-hm. What was it really like coming over? Trail of Tears, I think they came over.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They didn’t?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: They didn’t, they came later. I was just wondering what it was like. I wondered what it was like back then. It was a hardship for them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: I asked my grandmother what she thought about this in her heart. I asked her. She won’t say. [they laughed]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Myself, I feel a lot. Maybe, like, you both feel the same…a lot…sometimes we were hungry. We didn’t have what we wanted to eat, but we didn’t realize we were poor.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: That’s right! We thought we were doing good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s right. That’s what they were saying. But the rest of them thought we were poor, didn’t they? That’s what they said when they talked. I thought the same thing, too. I didn’t think we were poor. It was always good and we always laughed.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: It was that way everywhere.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: When we all lived by the water there’d be fish, crawdads, wild onions, and mushrooms. I thought we were eating good.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Me too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s right, have you had wild onions yet?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I’ve already had it once. I gathered some at the back of my house about 20 feet, we gathered it.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: That was good then. [laughed]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you have electricity in your home?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: No, not us.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How about water?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: There was a spring by the house.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is that where you got your water?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That was good water, wasn’t it?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Yes, it was.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It was good water from the spring.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about winter, what did you do to get through the winter?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: My dad raised hogs. He raised cows, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you kill the hogs?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you help him?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: I think so. [both laughed] I was small then.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When they said, “It’s time to eat,” you helped then? [laughing]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Grandpa had hogs, too, and raised a big garden and the same. And my mom canned everything. We had a lot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How did they store potatoes?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: I think in the cellar. They had hay in there and that’s where they stored them. They would throw them in there, [laughing] but they put them in there.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: He did the same. He kept it dark – it was dark inside.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s where he stored them?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They were good. They didn’t spoil?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: No, they even stored pig meat. They put a lot of salt on it. It stayed good. If they did that, it didn’t go rotten.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah. It gets too hot then, won’t it?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Grandpa had a smoke house, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He smoked it?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did it taste different when the meat was smoked?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: I don’t know. I didn’t pay attention to the taste. I just ate it. [they laughed]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: As long as you ate it. [laughing]

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: I was just waiting until it was time to eat.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Which one do think of more, your grandparents or your parents?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: My mother, I guess.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: My grandfather.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Your grandfather?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Myself my grandfather, just for a little while, and he died, what little I remember, I was the only one he brought candy to. He got on to the others. “Those are his! Don’t be eating up his candy,” he would say. That’s all I remember.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Of all your family, did your aunt and uncle live close by, or did they live somewhere else?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: They lived just where they were born. All of them on the 160 acres.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Right there?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was yours the same?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Uh-uh. They all lived different places.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: If there was anything to be done, did you all help one another?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: M-hm.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: All of you?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: M-hm. The Gadugi, that’s what they called it. If somebody needed wood they would cut wood for them. They all help each other. Someone needed help killing a hog, they would help them. Even calves.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I went down to Oak Grove Church one time. They build a fire in the ground. They put a cow in there. Then it was time to eat, they took it out. Did they do their cow like that?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-uh. The first time I saw it I went to the Housing Authority. I started the first week they dug a hole and they put a buffalo in there. And that’s the first time I had buffalo…

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you like it? Did you eat it?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Yeah, I ate it, but I didn’t like it. [Patsy laughs]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you go to school when you first began?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: The first time, but the school is not there now, that’s where I went to school at Lowery is what they called it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: After Lowery, where?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Oaks.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Four years?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When going to school, they didn’t forbid you to speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Uh-uh, it wasn’t like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh! A lot of them said it was like that.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: [Inaudible]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It wasn’t like that with you?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No? Where did you go to school?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: At Briggs. I went to first grade two times. [laughs] I went to first grade there, then I went to Sequoyah and that’s where I finished.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: My teacher was real nice. She watched over us all the time I think, and I guess you know about CCF (Children’s Christian Fund).

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Uh-huh, yeah.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: When we got that, then we all got on the bus went to buy clothes. They would take us there and he was nice to us. He was a white man teacher.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And I went to school a long ago. I was in the sixth grade and I don’t know how you would say this in Cherokee, but I was the teacher’s pet they would say. [they all laughed] That’s what I became. I was allowed to go to sleep in class and they wouldn’t say anything. [laughs] If they said anything, or they said, “He’s sleeping!” the teacher would say, “Leave him alone, let him sleep.” [all laughing] I went through sixth grade really good. [laughing]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you went to Sequoyah, did you live there or did you get to leave?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-uh, I just stayed there. It used to be that way, but not like that now.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: My sister, I don’t know if you know her or not? You might know her, Ruby.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Ruby Shell?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh. She was going to school there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Uh-huh. That’s where she went to school, yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How about... Do you remember Joe Tom Glass?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: He had already left.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He had already left? That’s where he went to school. His sister’s name is Viola.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Viola?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You remembered Viola?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, she went to school there. Three of my grandchildren, I think, finished school there. The last to finish was a boy. He was a quarterback for the football team.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The way we are speaking Cherokee, what do you think is going to happen?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: I really don’t know.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Hmm, I can’t say right now.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The way we are speaking now, do you think they will be speaking that way?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: No, I don’t think so. It’s just going away.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: They’re trying to learn to speak the language. There might be some left that speaks Cherokee. Very few.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: They are going to try to learn, which would be good, but I don’t think they are really trying. The little ones that are in school they go back to speaking English.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They got to speak it all the time.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: To really get good.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: I think that’s the way it has to be.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: They just forget it seems like.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: M-hm.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: My wife, she was a teacher. When they first started doing that, she was teaching. That’s the way it was. They would come in and go to school. When they got through, they went back to the same way, speaking English. I remember one, he learned real good, he came to speak real good. If it turns out like that it’s good, isn’t it?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s right.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was it like going to Sequoyah school?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: It was OK back then. This way was the boys’ dorm, and this way was the girls’ dorm, and there was a rec room. In the evening when they got there, they all gathered there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I guess they were all over?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is that what they did when they played, play football?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Hu uh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Already…

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-uh, football, basketball, baseball, track.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did you play?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Football and baseball.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Football and baseball, yeah. The one I was talking about played baseball. They gave him a scholarship, but then he quit. “Don’t do it,” I told him, “Don’t quit.” He quit, now he’s working highline poles they call it, he climbs them.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: I went to state in ’65 in Holdenville. They beat us and we got second place.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Football?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-uh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Baseball?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh, baseball.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What position did you play?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: First base and outfield.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So you played two places?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Weren’t you first when you went to Sequoyah?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Weren’t you?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Yep. Choate was the coach’s name back then, James Choate.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So…Did you go to state?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, that’s good.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: There’s just a few left of the boys that played.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That played?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you, did you play ball, Pat?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Basketball, basketball, and softball.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You played softball? Where did you play softball?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: There at Oaks, where I went to school.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about what they called independent, did you ever play?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It was funny back then. I played for a while, when they started fast pitching is when I quit. I couldn’t hit it. [they all laughed]

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: When it was fast pitch, I helped Dry Creek, for baseball, but for softball it was Greasy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No? Did you play with John Ross?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: M-hm, yep.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He played ball, too, John?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Um, little bit.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you have grandchildren?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many do you have? You mean you have a lot? [they all laugh]

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Seven of them.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: We have seven.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No, great-grandchildren?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Yes, I think I have…

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Three.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Yes, three.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I have seven grandchildren, and one is a great-granddaughter. But you wouldn’t think she’s Cherokee if you saw her. But because she’s spoiled, I was complaining all the time. She belongs to the White, I would say. I have one that’s that way, so I quit saying that.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: That’s the way it goes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It’s going to be more as we go. [they all laugh] I won’t be able to complain anymore. [laughs]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you were both growing up, when they hooked up electricity, what did you both think?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: I thought it was great when it came. [laughs] It wasn’t dark anymore. [all laughing] It was like daytime. [laughs]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You were all happy then?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it the same with water?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: huh?…

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When it came to the house?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: It was good. Yeah, I threw the bucket way out there. [all laughs]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about television, when you got it, what did you think?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: I couldn’t tell you, but I watched it all night long. [laughs]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Cartoons heh, Saturdays. [all laughs] You don’t think of anything? You might want to tell, you would think of? What your parents might have done or what they did? Do you both want to tell a little bit about it?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Uh hu. When I was already grown up, my grandfather help me and dad help me get a car. I’m happy he helped me out.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: My first car. [laughs]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He’s coming for you to help him, isn’t he? He’s going to come to you first. I see it the way I say it. They aren’t going to their parents. My grandchildren are going to come to me. It’s just like they treat me like a rich man, but you are going to do the same for all as far as you can go that we can help you. So, whatever their problem is, we are going to help them. That’s what I do.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: That’s the way it is now. [laugh]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Let’s say, in about 20 years, what do you think it’ll be like here on earth? What do you think it’ll be like? What do you think things are going to be like?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: There’s already automobiles that are electric and will be. But the weather, what’s happening now, it’s not four seasons anymore. It’s going to be warm.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I believe it’s going to get dry.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: I, myself, see it as warming up.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What do you think they should do now? The ones coming up that’s growing up? What do they need to do? During that time when all of this is happening, so they walk in good spirit here on earth?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: That’s right, going forward, one electric car [inaudible]. But about the weather, the pollution they talk about, they should have done something by now. I think they are trying. But then the rest of them are going a different way.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Pat, what do you think?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: I forget. It’s strange that we are living in the world now. There’s a lot going on, it’s a bad way.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It would help them if they went to school, isn’t that right?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: It’s scary when they learn.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: That’s right.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: What they would do.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Let’s go back there again. At Oaks, did you live at the school?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: There were some living there. But we rode the bus.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you went on the bus?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Uh huh. It stopped right here at my house.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many miles did you ride the bus?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: How far would it be? I guess 10 miles.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s the reason I’m asking you – it was still dark when I got on. [all laughing]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When I got to the high school, it was still dark. When I got home, it was already dark.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Uh-uh. It wasn’t that way with me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: With me, I rode the bus for a long time.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: They had a bus back then? [all laughing] Just one? [all laughing]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When I was going to school, they had four buses. But when I was going to Greasy, they had only two. They called it short run. They drop some of them off at the apartment first. [inaudible]…they come and get us. Myself, I really didn’t like going to school.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: And that’s right. [laughing]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: If they didn’t push me to go, I wouldn’t have gone to school. I wouldn’t know anything. I really don’t know anything right now. [laughing]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What’s coming now, do you think? Or what’s going to happen that would harm our children that’s coming up? Nothing coming to your mind?

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: You mean the children that are coming up?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: M-hm. What do you think is coming up that will be hard for them?

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: It’s already here. [laughing]

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: It’s already here what we have been waiting for.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It’s happening now.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: It’s already starting.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Now that we are finishing, maybe you two may want to say something. “I might want to say...I want to tell them,” you thinking.

segments.speaker: james-reese
segments.translation: Uh-huh, you are doing good, very good.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: You are doing good helping people. Also the Cherokee speakers, also good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Alright, if there’s nothing else, we are finished.

segments.speaker: patsy-reese
segments.translation: Wado.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I, too, am thankful for you two.
